1	import { useState, useCallback } from 'react'
2	import { PickFolder, ScanLocalRoot } from '../../../../wailsjs/go/main/App'
3	import { filetree } from '../../../../wailsjs/go/models'
4	import { LocalFile, LocalFileGroup } from '../types'
5	
6	// Flat, ordered list of every file in the tree (a group's own files, then
7	// its subgroups' files, recursively). Shared by the upload worker (order to
8	// process files in), the upload modal's per-group rollup counts, and the
9	// "every file in this group is done" check driving the Open-in-Drive link —
10	// one traversal so they can't drift out of sync on how they handle nesting.
11	export function flattenFiles(group: LocalFileGroup): LocalFile[] {
12	  return [...group.files, ...group.subgroups.flatMap(flattenFiles)]
13	}
14	
15	// Assigns every group's lookup key in one pass, right after a scan, so no
16	// consumer needs its own tree walk to rebuild it. `key` mirrors the tree's
17	// own nesting (parent key + '/' + name), rooted at null for the scan root.
18	// `group` is the shape ScanLocalRoot actually returns, before `key` exists.
19	function withKeys(group: filetree.LocalFileGroup, key: string | null): LocalFileGroup {
20	  return {
21	    ...group,
22	    key,
23	    subgroups: group.subgroups.map(sub => withKeys(sub, key === null ? sub.name : `${key}/${sub.name}`)),
24	  }
25	}
26	
27	export interface FileTreeHandle {
28	  root: string | null
29	  tree: LocalFileGroup | null
30	  loading: boolean
31	  error: string | null
32	  // Resolves to whether a folder was actually picked (false if the user
33	  // cancelled the dialog), so callers know when a fresh root replaced the
34	  // previous one and any per-root state (e.g. the upload queue) should reset.
35	  pickRoot: () => Promise<boolean>
36	}
37	
38	// Owns the currently scanned local folder: which root the user picked, the
39	// resulting file/subgroup tree, and loading/error state while ScanLocalRoot
40	// runs. The scan is an async Go RPC that can fail (bad permissions, folder
41	// moved/deleted mid-pick, etc.), so this state needs to live outside the
42	// tree itself — callers can show a spinner or an error message instead of
43	// rendering a stale or partial tree while a scan is in flight.
44	export function useFileTree(): FileTreeHandle {
45	  const [root, setRoot] = useState<string | null>(null)
46	  const [tree, setTree] = useState<LocalFileGroup | null>(null)
47	  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false)
48	  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null)
49	
50	  const pickRoot = useCallback(async () => {
51	    const folder = await PickFolder('Choose Root Folder')
52	    if (!folder) return false
53	
54	    setRoot(folder)
55	    setLoading(true)
56	    setError(null)
57	    try {
58	      setTree(withKeys(await ScanLocalRoot(folder), null))
59	    } catch (e) {
60	      setTree(null)
61	      setError(String(e))
62	    } finally {
63	      setLoading(false)
64	    }
65	    return true
66	  }, [])
67	
68	  return { root, tree, loading, error, pickRoot }
69	}

1	import { useRef, useState } from 'react'
2	import { handleUnexpectedError } from './globalErrorHandler'
3	
4	export interface AsyncActionHandle<Args extends unknown[]> {
5	  run: (...args: Args) => void
6	  pending: boolean
7	}
8	
9	// Wraps an async action (an RPC call, typically) so a trigger can't fire it
10	// again while a previous invocation from the same instance is still in
11	// flight, and so failures always surface through the same notification path
12	// instead of each call site catching (or forgetting to catch) errors on its
13	// own. `fn` is responsible for any state it wants to update on success; this
14	// hook only tracks whether it's in flight and reports failure.
15	export function useAsyncAction<Args extends unknown[]>(
16	  fn: (...args: Args) => Promise<void>,
17	  errorTitle?: string,
18	): AsyncActionHandle<Args> {
19	  const [pending, setPending] = useState(false)
20	  // Mirrors `pending` but reads synchronously, so a second call arriving
21	  // before React re-renders (state updates are batched) is still rejected.
22	  const pendingRef = useRef(false)
23	
24	  const run = (...args: Args) => {
25	    if (pendingRef.current) return
26	    pendingRef.current = true
27	    setPending(true)
28	    fn(...args)
29	      .catch(e => handleUnexpectedError(e, errorTitle))
30	      .finally(() => {
31	        pendingRef.current = false
32	        setPending(false)
33	      })
34	  }
35	
36	  return { run, pending }
37	}

This confirms it's still open. `AsyncButton`/`useAsyncAction` guards a *button instance* against re-entrant clicks (rejects a second call until the first settles), but that only blocks clicking "Choose root folder…" again while its own `pickRoot()` call is in flight — it doesn't add any correlation/token check inside `pickRoot` itself. Since `pickRoot` is called through this guard, in practice a user can't currently trigger two overlapping `pickRoot` calls from that one button — so the specific race the checklist item describes (button stays clickable mid-scan) is actually already prevented at the UI layer.

However, `checklist.md:134` is still unchecked, and `useFileTree.ts`'s `pickRoot` (lines 50–66) genuinely has no internal guard — if it were ever called from two places, or the button wrapper were removed, the second call could still win the race and leave root/tree mismatched (`root` and `tree` state aren't set atomically with a request token). So:

- **Symptom described in the checklist item (button stays clickable mid-scan) — no longer true**, since `AsyncButton` now disables it while pending.
- **Underlying lack of request correlation in `pickRoot` — still true**, it's just currently unreachable because the only caller is guarded externally.

So it's not fixed as written, but effectively mitigated by a different change (`AsyncButton`) that landed later without the checklist item being reconciled. Want me to update the checklist entry to reflect that, or leave it open since the internal guard is still genuinely missing?

When git gui rescans and populates its message box, it runs that hook, which overwrites the message file with its own `Entire-Checkpoint: ...` trailer before git gui reads it — clobbering whatever was written to `GITGUI_MSG`. User confirmed seeing `Entire-Checkpoint: ...` in the box instead of the drafted message. So `GITGUI_MSG` is no longer a reliable handoff channel in this repo; chat is the fallback. If Entire's behavior here ever changes (e.g. it starts preserving existing content, or a config flag suppresses the trailer), the `GITGUI_MSG` approach could be revisited.
14	
15	**How to apply:** Include the same trailer lines that would otherwise go via `-F`/`-m` (Co-Authored-By, Claude-Session) directly in the printed message so the user can copy the whole block as one paste — don't omit them expecting git gui or a hook to add them.
16	
17	**When this doesn't apply:** If the user explicitly asks me to run the actual `git commit` (e.g. no git gui in the loop, or a quick one-off), fall back to the older flow below: never commit without explicit confirmation that turn, show the drafted message first, then commit with `-F`.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Older flow (still applies when actually asked to run `git commit` myself)
22	
23	Never run `git commit` unless the user has explicitly asked for it in this turn. An earlier "commit" instruction does not authorize committing again later in the session — each commit (or batch of commits for one piece of work) needs its own explicit go-ahead. After finishing a reviewable chunk of work, stop and ask whether to commit; don't just do it because that's the rhythm the conversation fell into.
24	
25	**Why:** User corrected this on 2026-07-02: after saying "commit" once (for Step 2 work), I kept committing on my own for subsequent steps (Step 3a, a test-infra fix, Step 3b) without being asked again each time. This is about the approval relationship with this specific user — a different user of this repo might not want that friction at all — so it belongs in memory, not CLAUDE.md. See [[feedback_memory_vs_claudemd]].
26	
27	**How to apply:** Finish the work, run verification (build/test/typecheck), summarize what changed, and explicitly ask "want me to commit this?" — then wait. Do not commit proactively even if the previous turn's work was committed after a similar request. This applies within a single session and especially across multiple pieces of work in a row (e.g. a multi-step checklist implementation) — each step's commit needs its own confirmation, not just the first one. See also [[feedback_separate_commits]] for how to split what does get committed once confirmed.
28	
29	**Show the commit message first (added 2026-07-08):** Even once the user says "commit," show the drafted commit message in the chat turn first, then commit (in that same turn, no extra round-trip needed unless the user objects to the message). Why: user asked to see the message before it's used, so they can review/edit wording before it lands in history.
30	
31	**Use `git commit -F <file>`, not inline `-m "$(cat <<'EOF' ...)"` (added 2026-07-10):** Draft the message, write it to a scratchpad file with the Write tool, show its contents in chat as the preview, then run `git commit -F <path>`. Why: passing the message inline via a heredoc broke repeatedly whenever the message contained an apostrophe (`picker's`, `it's`) — something outside my own command also wraps the whole shell invocation in single quotes (likely a logging/sandboxing layer doing `eval '<command>'`), and a literal apostrophe anywhere in the text prematurely closes that outer quoting since single quotes can't be escaped from within themselves. Writing the message to a file sidesteps shell quoting entirely — apostrophes, quotes, backticks are all safe in file content. `-F` also naturally satisfies the "show the message first" rule above, since the file is written (and can be shown) before the commit runs. This is purely a workaround for how *I* invoke shell commands in this sandboxed environment — not relevant to a human contributor or a rule about repo content — so it's memory, not CLAUDE.md.
32	
33	**Skip `git status` / `git add`, pass pathspecs straight to `git commit` (added 2026-07-10):** Default commit command is now `git commit -F <message-file> -- <path1> <path2> ...`, listing exactly the files touched this turn. `git commit <pathspec>` stages and commits only those paths' current working-tree content, regardless of what else is dirty elsewhere — no preceding `git add` needed. `git status` is skippable too since I already know which files I edited from my own tool calls this session; I don't need to discover that via status. Why: user asked for a leaner commit flow after watching the status→add→commit dance every time. Caveat: this repo has had stray unrelated modified files show up before (e.g. `frontend/wailsjs/runtime/*` regenerated by a `wails dev` run outside the session) — always naming explicit paths on `git commit` is what keeps those out, so don't switch to `git commit -a` or `git add -A` even though they'd also skip the status/add dance.
